## 1. Problem setup: comparing two group means

The `Income.dat` dataset records annual income, years of education, and
racial group for a sample of adults in the United States. Income is
reported in thousands of US dollars; the race group codes are `B`
(Black), `H` (Hispanic), and `W` (White).

We focus on two groups:

-   **Group X (Black):** 16 observations, coded `B`.

-   **Group Y (Hispanic):** 14 observations, coded `H`.

We will test whether there is a statistically significant difference in
the population mean annual income between Black and Hispanic adults.

**Problem statement.** Using the observed incomes for groups `B` and
`H`, test whether their population mean annual incomes differ at the 5%
significance level.

Let $\mu_X$ and $\mu_Y$ denote the population mean annual incomes for
the two groups, respectively.

We wish to test

$$
H_0:\mu_X=\mu_Y
\quad\text{versus}\quad
H_a:\mu_X\neq\mu_Y
$$

at significance level $\alpha=0.05$.

We will investigate this question using three approaches: a likelihood
ratio test (LRT), a pooled two-sample $t$-test, and a permutation test.

```{r read-data}
source_file <- "https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/Income.dat"
data <- read.table(source_file, header = TRUE)
x <- data$income[data$race == "B"]
y <- data$income[data$race == "H"]
nX <- length(x)
nY <- length(y)
N <- nX + nY
table(data$race)
```

```{r group-summary}
summary_by_group <- data |>
  filter(race %in% c("B", "H")) |>
  group_by(race) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(income),
    median = median(income),
    sd = sd(income)
  )

knitr::kable(summary_by_group, digits = 3)
```

```{r exploratory-plots, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5, out.width="\\textwidth", fig.align="center"}

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

# 1. Raw data
stripchart(list(B = x, H = y),
           method = "jitter", vertical = TRUE,
           pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
           main = "Raw Income Data",
           xlab = "Group", ylab = "Income ($1,000s)")

# 2. Boxplots
boxplot(list(B = x, H = y),
        col = "lightblue",
        main = "Income by Group",
        xlab = "Group", ylab = "Income ($1,000s)")

# 3. Normal Q-Q plot for group 1
qqnorm(x, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot: B")
qqline(x, col = "red")

# 4. Normal Q-Q plot for group 2
qqnorm(y, main = "Normal Q-Q Plot: H")
qqline(y, col = "red")

```

> **Discussion:** Are there outliers, skewness, or major differences in
> spread?

## 2. Likelihood ratio test (LRT)

### 2.1 Model, hypotheses and dimensions

Assume independent normal samples with *unknown but common* variance:

$$
X_1,\ldots,X_{n_X}\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu_X,\sigma^2),\qquad
Y_1,\ldots,Y_{n_Y}\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu_Y,\sigma^2).
$$

Test

$$
H_0:\mu_X=\mu_Y\qquad\text{versus}\qquad H_a:\mu_X\ne\mu_Y.
$$

Denote the parameters as $\theta$: $\theta=(\mu_X,\mu_Y,\sigma^2)$. Then
the full parameter space and the null parameter space are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Omega&=\{(\mu_X,\mu_Y,\sigma^2):\mu_X,\mu_Y\in\mathbb R,\ \sigma^2>0\},
&\dim(\Omega)&=3,\\
\omega_0&=\{(\mu,\mu,\sigma^2):\mu\in\mathbb R,\ \sigma^2>0\},
&\dim(\omega_0)&=2.
\end{aligned}
$$

### 2.2 Log-likelihood

The log-likelihood is $$
\ell(\mu_X,\mu_Y,\sigma^2)=
-\frac N2\log(2\pi\sigma^2)-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{n_X}(X_i-\mu_X)^2+\sum_{j=1}^{n_Y}(Y_j-\mu_Y)^2\right].
$$

### 2.3 MLEs

We know that the unrestricted MLEs are $$
\hat\mu_X=\bar X, \quad \hat\mu_Y=\bar Y, \quad\hat\sigma^2=\frac{1}{N}[\sum_{i=1}^{n_X}(X_i-\hat\mu_X)^2+\sum_{j=1}^{n_Y}(Y_j-\hat\mu_Y)^2].
$$

Under $H_0$ the data are fit with one common mean, so $$
\hat\mu_0
=\frac{n_X\bar X+n_Y\bar Y}{N},
\quad\hat\sigma_0^2=\frac{1}{N}[\sum_{i=1}^{n_X}(X_i-\hat\mu_0)^2+\sum_{j=1}^{n_Y}(Y_j-\hat\mu_0)^2].
$$

```{r calculate-mles}
mean_X <- mean(x)
mean_Y <- mean(y)
mean_0 <- mean(c(x, y))

SSX <- sum((x - mean_X)^2)
SSY <- sum((y - mean_Y)^2)
sigma2_MLE_full <- (SSX + SSY) / N
sigma2_MLE_null <- (sum((x - mean_0)^2) + sum((y - mean_0)^2)) / N

mle_summary <- data.frame(
  model = c("Full", "Null"),
  mu_X = c(mean_X, mean_0),
  mu_Y = c(mean_Y, mean_0),
  sigma2 = c(sigma2_MLE_full, sigma2_MLE_null)
)
knitr::kable(mle_summary, 
             digits = 4, 
             caption = "MLEs in full parameter space and null parameter space")
```

### 2.4 Likelihood ratio statistic

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Lambda
&=2\left[\sup_{\theta\in\Omega}\ell(\theta)
-\sup_{\theta\in\omega_0}\ell(\theta)\right]\\
&=2\left[-\frac N2\log(2\pi\widehat\sigma^2)-\frac N2
 +\frac N2\log(2\pi\widehat\sigma_0^2)+\frac N2\right]\\
 &=N\log\left(\frac{\widehat\sigma_0^2}{\widehat\sigma^2}\right)
\geq 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

> **Discussion:** Why $\Lambda \ge 0$?

### 2.5 Asymptotic $\chi^2$ inference

Under regularity conditions and $H_0$, $\Lambda\xrightarrow{D}\chi^2_1$
as sample sizes increase. Thus for significance level $\alpha=0.05$, the
approximate critical value and p-value are $$
c_{\alpha,\mathrm{asymp}}=\chi^2_{1,1-\alpha},\quad
\text{asymptotic p-value}=P(\chi_1^2\ge\Lambda_{\rm obs}).
$$

```{r asymptotic-lrt}
alpha <- 0.05
lambda_obs <- N * log(sigma2_MLE_null / sigma2_MLE_full)
p_LRT_asymp <- pchisq(lambda_obs, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
crit_val_LRT_asymp <- qchisq(1 - alpha, df = 1)

c(LR_statistic = lambda_obs, p_value_asymptotic = p_LRT_asymp,
  critical_value_asymp = crit_val_LRT_asymp)
```

The asymptotic p-value is about $0.4836$, which is **greater than**
$\alpha=0.05$. Thus we **fail to reject** $H_0$. This does not establish
that the two population means are equal.

## 3. Pooled two-sample $t$-test

Assume independent normal samples with *unknown but common* variance:

$$
X_1,\ldots,X_{n_X}\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu_X,\sigma^2),\qquad
Y_1,\ldots,Y_{n_Y}\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(\mu_Y,\sigma^2).
$$ Define the pooled sample variance $$
s_p^2 =
\frac{(n_X-1)s_X^2+(n_Y-1)s_Y^2}{n_X+n_Y-2}.
$$ The t-statistic is $$
T=\frac{(\bar X-\bar Y)-0}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_X+1/n_Y}}.
$$ Under $H_0$, $T\sim t_{N-2}$. Hence the critical value and p-value
are $$
c_{\alpha} = t_{N-2, 1-\alpha/2}, \qquad
\text{p-value}=P_{H_0}(|T|\geq |t_{obs}|).
$$

```{r pooled-t-test}
sp2 <- (SSX + SSY) / (N - 2)
t_obs <- (mean_X - mean_Y) / sqrt(sp2 * (1 / nX + 1 / nY))
df_t <- N - 2

p_t_manual <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_obs), df = df_t)
crit_val_t <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df = df_t)

c(t_statistic = t_obs,
  p_value = p_t_manual, 
  critical_value = crit_val_t)

# The default t.test() uses Welch's test; we explicitly request pooled variance.
t_test <- t.test(x, y, alternative = "two.sided", var.equal = TRUE)
t_test
```

## 4. Relationship between the LRT and the pooled $t$-test

For group $X$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n_X}(X_i-\hat\mu_0)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^{n_X}\big[(X_i-\bar X)+(\bar X-\hat\mu_0)\big]^2\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^{n_X}(X_i-\bar X)^2+n_X(\bar X-\hat\mu_0)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly for group $Y$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=1}^{n_Y}(Y_i-\hat\mu_0)^2
&=\sum_{i=1}^{n_Y}(Y_i-\bar Y)^2+n_Y(\bar Y-\hat\mu_0)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence

$$
\hat\sigma_0^2
=
\hat\sigma^2+
\frac1N\left[
n_X(\bar X-\hat\mu_0)^2
+n_Y(\bar Y-\hat\mu_0)^2
\right].
$$

Now, using the definition of $\hat\mu_0$, $$
\begin{aligned}
\bar X-\hat\mu_0
&=\bar X-\frac{n_X\bar X+n_Y\bar Y}{N}\\
&=\frac{n_Y}{N}(\bar X-\bar Y).
\end{aligned}
$$ Likewise, $$
\bar Y-\hat\mu_0
=-\frac{n_X}{N}(\bar X-\bar Y).
$$ Substituting,$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\sigma_0^2
&=\hat\sigma^2+
\frac1N\left[
n_X\frac{n_Y^2}{N^2}(\bar X-\bar Y)^2+
n_Y\frac{n_X^2}{N^2}(\bar X-\bar Y)^2
\right]\\[4pt]
&=\hat\sigma^2+
\frac{n_Xn_Y(n_X+n_Y)}{N^3}
(\bar X-\bar Y)^2\\
&=\hat\sigma^2+
\frac{n_Xn_Y}{N^2}
(\bar X-\bar Y)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$ Recall that the pooled two-sample $t$-statistic is $$
T=\frac{\bar X-\bar Y}
{s_p\sqrt{\frac1{n_X}+\frac1{n_Y}}},
$$ where $$
s_p^2=
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{n_X}(X_i-\bar X)^2+
\sum_{j=1}^{n_Y}(Y_j-\bar Y)^2
}{N-2}.
$$

Notice that $s_p^2$ and $\hat\sigma^2$ have the same numerator but
different denominators. Therefore, $$
\hat\sigma^2=\frac{N-2}{N}s_p^2.
$$ Next, square the $t$-statistic: $$
\begin{aligned}
T^2
&=\frac{(\bar X-\bar Y)^2}
{s_p^2\left(\frac1{n_X}+\frac1{n_Y}\right)}\\[4pt]
&=\frac{n_Xn_Y(\bar X-\bar Y)^2}{Ns_p^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ Rearranging, $$
\frac{n_Xn_Y}{N^2}(\bar X-\bar Y)^2
=\frac{T^2s_p^2}{N}.
$$ Substitute this into our expression for $\hat\sigma_0^2$: $$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\sigma_0^2
&=\hat\sigma^2+\frac{T^2s_p^2}{N}\\[4pt]
&=\frac{N-2}{N}s_p^2+\frac{T^2s_p^2}{N}\\[4pt]
&=\frac{s_p^2}{N}(N-2+T^2).
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\hat\sigma_0^2}{\hat\sigma^2}
&=\frac{\frac{s_p^2}{N}(N-2+T^2)}
{\frac{N-2}{N}s_p^2}\\[4pt]
&=\frac{N-2+T^2}{N-2}\\[4pt]
&=1+\frac{T^2}{N-2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that $$
\Lambda=N\log\left(\frac{\hat\sigma_0^2}{\hat\sigma^2}\right).
$$

We obtain $$
\Lambda=N\log\left(1+\frac{T^2}{N-2}\right).
$$

The function $$
f(t)=N\log\left(1+\frac{t^2}{N-2}\right)
$$ is strictly increasing in $|t|$ for $N>2$.

Therefore, $$
\Lambda\text{ is large}
\iff |T|\text{ is large}.
$$

Both tests reject $H_0$ when the difference between the sample means is
sufficiently large relative to the estimated standard error. Under the
normal model and $H_0$,

$$
T\sim t_{N-2}.
$$ Hence the exact p-value for the LRT can be calculated using the
$t$-distribution:

$$
\text{p-value}=2P_{H_0}(T > |t_{\mathrm{obs}}|).
$$ Equivalently, if only the observed LRT statistic
$\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}$ is known, we can recover

$$
|t_{\mathrm{obs}}|
=
\sqrt{(N-2)\left(e^{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}/N}-1\right)}.
$$

The exact level-$\alpha$ critical value for the LRT is


$$
c_\alpha
=
N\log\left(
1+\frac{t_{N-2,\,1-\alpha/2}^2}{N-2}
\right).
$$


Thus, the exact LRT and the two-sided pooled $t$-test produce identical
p-values and rejection decisions. In contrast, the $\chi^2_1$
approximation does *not* produce exactly the same finite-sample p-value
or critical value.

```{r verify-lrt-t}
lambda_from_t <- N * log1p(abs(t_obs)^2 / (N - 2))

# Transform the exact two-sided t critical value to the LRT scale
crit_val_LRT_exact <- N * log1p(crit_val_t^2 / (N - 2))

abs_t_from_Lambda <- sqrt((N - 2) * expm1(lambda_obs / N))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(lambda_obs, lambda_from_t, tolerance = 1e-10)))
p_LRT_exact <- 2 * pt(-abs_t_from_Lambda, df = df_t)

comparison <- data.frame(
  method = c("LRT, chi-squared approximation",
             "LRT, exact t calibration",
             "Pooled t-test, exact"),
  statistic = c(lambda_obs, lambda_from_t, abs(t_obs)),
  critical_value = c(crit_val_LRT_asymp, crit_val_LRT_exact, crit_val_t),
  p_value = c(p_LRT_asymp, p_LRT_exact, p_t_manual)
)
knitr::kable(comparison, digits = 5)
```

Note that the first two rows use the **LRT statistic** while the last
row uses $|T|$. Their critical values are therefore on different scales.
The exact LRT calibration and the pooled $t$-test have identical
p-values.

## 5. Permutation test

The normal-model LRT and pooled $t$-test rely on model assumptions for
their reference distributions. A classical two-sample permutation test
avoids a normality assumption, but it needs *exchangeability* under
its null hypothesis.

For two independent samples from distributions $F_X$ and $F_Y$, one
sufficient permutation null hypothesis for this problem is

$$
H_0: F_X=F_Y.
$$

Under this stronger null, the pooled observations are identically distributed and the group labels are exchangeable. Conditional on the
observed income values and the fixed sizes $n_X$ and $n_Y$, each allocation of
$n_X$ entries to group `B` (and the remaining $n_Y$ to group `H`) is equally
likely. This tests the stronger equality-of-distributions null, using a
statistic sensitive to differences in means.

*Notes*. The original question concerns equality of population *means*. Equality of means alone does not imply exchangeability or identical distributions. The classical label-permutation test is exact under the stronger exchangeability null, not automatically for an arbitrary means-only null.

We use the absolute value of the pooled $t$-statistic,

$$
T_0=\frac{|\bar X-\bar Y|}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_X+1/n_Y}}.
$$

We keep income values fixed and redistribute the `B`/`H` labels, preserving
the number in each group.

```{r permutation-test}
# Calculate the absolute pooled t-statistic for two vectors of incomes.
abs_pooled_t <- function(a, b) {
  na <- length(a)
  nb <- length(b)
  sse <- sum((a - mean(a))^2) + sum((b - mean(b))^2)
  sp2_star <- sse / (na + nb - 2)
  abs(mean(a) - mean(b)) / sqrt(sp2_star * (1 / na + 1 / nb))
}

z <- c(x, y)
set.seed(135)
B <- 10000
t_perm <- replicate(B, {
  # Choose nX of the N observed pooled entries WITHOUT replacement.
  chosen <- sample.int(N, size = nX, replace = FALSE)
  x_star <- z[chosen]
  y_star <- z[-chosen]
  abs_pooled_t(x_star, y_star)
})

p_perm <- mean(t_perm >= abs(t_obs))

c(observed_abs_t = abs(t_obs),
  extreme_permutations = sum(t_perm >= abs(t_obs)),
  p = p_perm)
```

```{r permutation-histogram, fig.width=7, fig.height=5.5, out.width="\\textwidth", fig.align="center"}
hist(t_perm, breaks = 45, freq = FALSE,
     main = "Permutation null distribution of |t|",
     xlab = "Absolute pooled t-statistic under shuffled labels",
     col = "grey85", border = "white")
abline(v = abs(t_obs), col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", legend = sprintf("Observed |t| = %.3f", abs(t_obs)),
       col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

```{r compare-permutation}

crit_val_perm_approx <- unname(
  quantile(t_perm, probs = 1 - alpha, type = 1)
)

comparison <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Pooled t-test",
    "LRT (asymptotic)",
    "Permutation test"
  ),
  Statistic = c(abs(t_obs), lambda_obs, abs(t_obs)),
  `p-value` = c(p_t_manual, p_LRT_asymp, p_perm),
  `5% critical value` = c(
    crit_val_t, crit_val_LRT_asymp, crit_val_perm_approx
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  comparison,
  digits = 4,
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption = "Comparison of hypothesis tests"
)

```
